subject_line: Gemma Sullivan and the cottage in Mimico
email_body:
Dear Jeanette,

The Paper Birds puts Canada's wartime women codebreakers at its centre, with Gemma Sullivan recruited into a secret unit working out of a lakeside cottage in Mimico, near a POW camp. Congratulations, too, on the Fiction Award at the 2026 Saskatchewan Book Awards.

We would love to ask how you came to this nearly unrecorded corner of the Second World War, and how directing the MFA in Writing in Saskatoon sits alongside writing a fourth novel.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. Each portrait is developed through a few written questions you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part?

Best regards,

subject_line: Writing a serial long poem in Myself a Paperclip
email_body:
Dear Triny,

Myself a Paperclip takes on mental illness and stigma as a single serial long poem rather than a collection of separate lyrics, and it went on to win the 2022 Fiddlehead Poetry Prize. I was also interested to see a chapbook, Finding the Love You Need, appear in 2025.

We would like to ask why the long poem was the right form for this material, and how teaching creative writing at UNB in Fredericton shapes the way you think about sequence and form.

subject_line: The circus sideshows of The Last Show on Earth
email_body:
Dear Yvonne,

In The Last Show on Earth you set everyday people and moments inside a circus, as sideshows and exhibitions of the unusual, and use that frame to think about death, disability and the Anthropocene. Poems like "Circus Moon, Circus Train" and "Sad sonnet with an extra couplet" stayed with me.

We would like to ask how the circus became your lens for an imperilled world, and how your years as Victoria's Poet Laureate and with Planet Earth Poetry fed into the book.

subject_line: The body as a house in I used to live here
email_body:
Dear Amy,

I used to live here turns to chronic illness, disability and autoimmunity, and the Open Book piece on it framed the collection around a body that no longer feels like a home. That image seems to echo the Gothic domestic spaces of your story collection Homebodies.

We would like to ask whether the house has always been your way into the body, and how moving between poetry, the novella Unlocking and linked stories shapes what each form lets you say.

subject_line: Ebele's bicycle wish in Wish Maker
email_body:
Dear Uchechukwu,

Wish Maker follows nine-year-old Ebele through a Christmas week in a riverine village in southeast Nigeria, wanting a bicycle his widowed mother cannot afford and meeting a smelly, irritating stranger who insists he is an angel. Your Isele interview about Double Wahala, Double Trouble, and how "Neighbours" handles domestic abuse with humour, suggested a similar instinct for mixing lightness and weight.

We would like to ask how writing for young readers from Calgary keeps you connected to those Nigerian settings.

subject_line: Estelle et les évasions de L'Équilibre
email_body:
Bonjour Cassie,

Dans L'Équilibre, dix ans après l'instauration d'un système de punition novateur, l'heure est à la réforme, et Estelle doit comprendre par quelles failles les prisonniers s'évadent, alors même que sa compagne est gravement malade. Ce polar dystopique fait tenir ensemble la responsabilité collective et l'intime.

Nous aimerions vous demander comment ce roman est né, et comment votre enseignement des théories de la fiction et de la narrativité à l'UQAM nourrit votre propre écriture.

The Author Ledger est un projet indépendant qui publie de courts portraits d'auteurs. Chaque portrait se construit à partir de quelques questions écrites, auxquelles vous répondez à votre rythme, et le texte complet vous est soumis pour relecture avant publication.

Seriez-vous partante pour y participer ?

Bien cordialement,
The Author Ledger

subject_line: Climate and surveillance on stage in Watchlist
email_body:
Dear Alex,

Watchlist takes on climate change and surveillance together, which is a striking pairing for a play, and it sits alongside Out of the Ordinary in your Currency Press list. I was also curious to read that your debut, Once Upon a Midnight, was a bilingual horror rock musical that premiered in Okinawa before reaching Adelaide's OzAsia Festival.

We would like to ask how you choose between the stage and prose for an idea, now that you are also writing fiction alongside teaching at Flinders.

subject_line: Grief, autism and Darwin in White Noise
email_body:
Dear Raelke,

White Noise is a YA novel about grief and autism set in Darwin, a city that rarely gets to be the backdrop for young adult fiction. In your Write & Seek conversation you talked about authentic neurodivergent representation and about the tropes that keep repeating in YA.

We would like to ask which of those tropes you set out to avoid in White Noise, and how Darwin's climate and rhythms shaped the story, alongside your teaching of creative writing at Charles Darwin University.

subject_line: From Hazelwood's 45 days to the preppers
email_body:
Dear Tom,

Hazelwood reconstructs the 45-day mine fire near Morwell from roughly 95 interviews with Latrobe Valley residents, and traces the decisions back to the 1920s, despite legal hold-ups that delayed publication until 2020. Your current project, We Are All Preppers Now, about survivalists, climate activists and other subcultures of imminent collapse, seems to grow out of the same territory.

We would like to ask how listening to a town in crisis changed the way you approach collapse as a subject.
